question: Guess a quantity, then guess it again three weeks later and average the two. How does that average usually compare?
options: No better than the first guess
answer: Better than the first guess. Vul and Pashler found in 2008 that averaging two guesses from the same person beat either one alone, and that a three-week gap helped more than guessing twice at once. Each guess carries its own random error, and averaging cancels part of it: a crowd of one, but a crowd.
move: Sleep on an estimate, then average the two answers.
ask: Before my next big estimate, of cost or time, could I guess twice and take the middle?
trap: No better, since both guesses come from the same head.
reference: Vul & Pashler, Measuring the crowd within: probabilistic representations within individuals, Psychological Science 19:645–647, 2008
